newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Fresh shelling, mediation talks in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Fresh shelling, mediation talks in Brazzaville.

text.p: A fierce bout of shelling rocked the centre of the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville on Thursday as its mayor held more talks on ending a bloody month-long showdown there, witnesses said.
Mayor Bernard Kolelas met former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso to try to persuade him to accept a nine-point peace plan, a spokesman said.

The spokesman, Hellot Mampouya, said earlier that President Pascal Lissouba, whose forces have been fighting Sassou militia for control of the city centre and international airport, had accepted the plan on Tuesday as a basis for negotiation.

"Lissouba considered the nine points were suitable for discussion and said he accepted them as a basis for talks," Mampouya said during a lull that followed heavy evening exchanges of shellfire on Wednesday.
Witnesses said Thursday afternoon's exchange was around the city centre front line. It was unclear who started firing.
The nine-point plan centres on conditions for presidential elections that had been scheduled for July 27 before fighting broke out on June 5.
Both parties in the conflict have more or less admitted that date is no longer feasible but the presidential poll has not officially been cancelled.
"It would be absolutely surrealistic to hold elections July 27, unless you're talking about July 27, 1998," one Western diplomat told Reuters.
Mampouya said Kolelas's meetings concerned the nine-point plan and did not extend to proposals made by Gabonese President Omar Bongo, the international mediator in the conflict.
Bongo is trying to negotiate a ceasefire from Saturday.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said on Wednesday he would ask the Security Council to endorse an African peacekeeping force for the Congo and for the group's wealthier members to pay for it.

"Since neither side trusts the other, both want a peacekeeping force which could supervise a ceasefire and secure the airport to make sure weapons do not flow into the country," he told Reuters. He was due to meet council members Thursday.
There have been several truces in the showdown, in which indiscriminate shooting and shellfire has killed hundreds of innocent civilians. None has held much longer than 24 hours.
Kolelas's supporters were in the thick of similar political and ethnic clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 and early 1994 after disputed parliamentary elections.
They have stayed out of the fighting this time and their Bacongo stronghold is home to tens of thousands of displaced persons who have fled other parts of town.

The current conflict erupted on June 5 when troops loyal to Lissouba surrounded Sassou's residence with the ostensible aim of arresting supporters blamed for a series of killings in the north of the country. The move was part of efforts to disband private militias ahead of the election.
